claim: In 2017, 22% of all deaths among adults were attributed to dietary risks with type 2 diabetes being among the top causes of diet-related deaths.
source: In 2017, 22% of all deaths among adults were attributed to dietary risks with type 2 diabetes being among the top causes of diet-related deaths (Collaborators, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Collaborators, 2019.

claim: Urinary metabolic phenotypes carry rich information on environmental, lifestyle and nutritional exposures, physiological and metabolic status, and disease risks on an individual and population level.
source: Urinary metabolic phenotypes carry rich information on environmental, lifestyle and nutritional exposures, physiological and metabolic status, and disease risks on an individual and population level (Gibson et al., 2020; Collins et al., 2019; Rebholz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gibson et al., 2020; Collins et al., 2019; Rebholz et al., 2018.

claim: Urine specimens have high concentrations of food-derived metabolites.
source: Urine specimens have high concentrations of food-derived metabolites and studies have shown that urinary metabolic profiles could provide an objective measure of dietary intake (O'Gorman and Brennan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Gorman and Brennan, 2017.

claim: Studies have shown that urinary metabolic profiles could provide an objective measure of dietary intake.
source: Urine specimens have high concentrations of food-derived metabolites and studies have shown that urinary metabolic profiles could provide an objective measure of dietary intake (O'Gorman and Brennan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Gorman and Brennan, 2017.

claim: Previous research identifying diet-related metabolic profiles has largely focused on selected food groups including fruits, vegetables, meat, and seafood.
source: Previous research identifying diet-related metabolic profiles has largely focused on selected food groups including fruits, vegetables, meat, and seafood (Gibson et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2018; Guertin et al., 2014; Playdon et al., 2016; Scalbert et al., 2014), while dietary patterns and food processing are far less studied (Collins et al., 2019; Rebholz et al., 2018; Garcia-Perez et al., 2017; Martinez et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gibson et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2018; Guertin et al., 2014; Playdon et al., 2016; Scalbert et al., 2014.

claim: Dietary patterns and food processing are far less studied than selected food groups.
source: Previous research identifying diet-related metabolic profiles has largely focused on selected food groups including fruits, vegetables, meat, and seafood (Gibson et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2018; Guertin et al., 2014; Playdon et al., 2016; Scalbert et al., 2014), while dietary patterns and food processing are far less studied (Collins et al., 2019; Rebholz et al., 2018; Garcia-Perez et al., 2017; Martinez et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2019; Rebholz et al., 2018; Garcia-Perez et al., 2017; Martinez et al., 2016.

claim: UPF consumption has been increasing worldwide.
source: UPF consumption has been increasing worldwide (Monteiro et al., 2013; Monteiro et al., 2018a; Monteiro et al., 2018b; Baker et al., 2020) and, to our knowledge, no previous report exists on its metabolic signature.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Monteiro et al., 2013; Monteiro et al., 2018a; Monteiro et al., 2018b; Baker et al., 2020.

claim: No previous report exists on the metabolic signature of UPF consumption.
source: UPF consumption has been increasing worldwide (Monteiro et al., 2013; Monteiro et al., 2018a; Monteiro et al., 2018b; Baker et al., 2020) and, to our knowledge, no previous report exists on its metabolic signature.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: Age is a major source of variation in metabolite profiling, with large differences being observed between children and adults.
source: This is important as age is a major source of variation in metabolite profiling, with large differences being observed between children and adults (Ellul et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ellul et al., 2019.

claim: Alterations in the levels of several metabolic biomarkers and pathways have been associated with insulin resistance in childhood including branched-chain and aromatic amino acid metabolism, urea cycle, glucose, and carbohydrate metabolism.
source: Alterations in the levels of several metabolic biomarkers and pathways have been associated with insulin resistance in childhood including branched-chain and aromatic amino acid metabolism, urea cycle, glucose, and carbohydrate metabolism (Rauschert et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2016; Martos-Moreno et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rauschert et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2016; Martos-Moreno et al., 2017.

claim: Dietary patterns characterized by high consumption of UPFs, such soft drinks, sweet, and savoury snacks, have been related to higher risk of insulin resistance in children.
source: In addition, dietary patterns characterized by high consumption of UPFs, such soft drinks, sweet, and savoury snacks, have been related to higher risk of insulin resistance in children (Karatzi et al., 2014; Romero-Polvo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karatzi et al., 2014; Romero-Polvo et al., 2012.

claim: C-peptide is a protein that is cosecreted with insulin on an equimolar basis from pancreatic β-cells.
source: An alternative marker is C‐peptide, a protein that is cosecreted with insulin on an equimolar basis from pancreatic β-cells and has been shown to strongly predict metabolic disease progression (Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2012.

claim: C-peptide has been shown to strongly predict metabolic disease progression.
source: An alternative marker is C‐peptide, a protein that is cosecreted with insulin on an equimolar basis from pancreatic β-cells and has been shown to strongly predict metabolic disease progression (Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2012.

claim: C-peptide has a longer half‐life than insulin.
source: C-peptide has a longer half‐life than insulin and is recognized as a stable and accurate marker of endogenous insulin secretion, even in nonfasting conditions (Hope et al., 2016; Vezzosi et al., 2007; Polonsky et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hope et al., 2016; Vezzosi et al., 2007; Polonsky et al., 1986.

claim: C-peptide is recognized as a stable and accurate marker of endogenous insulin secretion, even in nonfasting conditions.
source: C-peptide has a longer half‐life than insulin and is recognized as a stable and accurate marker of endogenous insulin secretion, even in nonfasting conditions (Hope et al., 2016; Vezzosi et al., 2007; Polonsky et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hope et al., 2016; Vezzosi et al., 2007; Polonsky et al., 1986.

claim: Previous studies in children have shown that higher carbohydrate intake is related to higher C-peptide concentrations.
source: Previous studies in children have shown that higher carbohydrate intake is related to higher C-peptide concentrations (Sunehag et al., 2002; Buyken et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sunehag et al., 2002; Buyken et al., 2006.

claim: The study population consisted of 1147 children with available information on dietary intake, plasma C-peptide levels, and metabolomic biomarkers in urine collected during the HELIX follow-up at a mean age of 7.9 years (range: 5.4–12.0 years).
source: Our study population consisted of 1147 children with available information on dietary intake, plasma C-peptide levels, and metabolomic biomarkers in urine collected during the HELIX follow-up at a mean age of 7.9 years (range: 5.4–12.0 years) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Among participating children (n = 1147), 626 (54.6%) were boys and 1028 (89.6%) were white.
source: Among participating children (n = 1147), 626 (54.6%) were boys and 1028 (89.6%) were white (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The mean (SD) age at assessment was 7.9 (1.6) years.
source: The mean (SD) age at assessment was 7.9 (1.6) years.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Median (IQR) C-peptide concentration was 1.26 (0.03, 1.95) ng/ml.
source: Median (IQR) C-peptide concentration was 1.26 (0.03, 1.95) ng/ml.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Seventeen percent of children (n = 195) had a high KIDMED score (>4), indicative of high adherence to the Mediterranean diet.
source: Seventeen percent of children (n = 195) had a high KIDMED score (>4), indicative of high adherence to the Mediterranean diet.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Mean (SD) UPF intake in the overall study population was 24.2 (8.7)% of total daily food intake.
source: Mean (SD) UPF intake in the overall study population was 24.2 (8.7)% of total daily food intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: KIDMED and UPF intake were negatively correlated (Spearman r = −0.44).
source: KIDMED and UPF intake were negatively correlated (Spearman r = −0.44); children with high and low (<1) KIDMED score had a mean (SD) UPF intake of 18.8 (6.6)% and 33.4 (9.9)%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Children with high KIDMED score had a mean (SD) UPF intake of 18.8 (6.6)%.
source: KIDMED and UPF intake were negatively correlated (Spearman r = −0.44); children with high and low (<1) KIDMED score had a mean (SD) UPF intake of 18.8 (6.6)% and 33.4 (9.9)%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Children with low (<1) KIDMED score had a mean (SD) UPF intake of 33.4 (9.9)%.
source: KIDMED and UPF intake were negatively correlated (Spearman r = −0.44); children with high and low (<1) KIDMED score had a mean (SD) UPF intake of 18.8 (6.6)% and 33.4 (9.9)%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Daily fruit and vegetable consumption, weekly fish consumption and not skipping breakfast were the major dietary habits differentiating children with low and high KIDMED score.
source: Daily fruit and vegetable consumption, weekly fish consumption and not skipping breakfast were the major dietary habits differentiating children with low and high KIDMED score (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Intakes of pastries and bakery products, dairy desserts, margarine, and dressings were the major determinants of UPF intake.
source: Intakes of pastries and bakery products, dairy desserts, margarine, and dressings were the major determinants of UPF intake (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: Children with the highest KIDMED scores were mostly from Norway and Spain.
source: Children with the highest KIDMED scores were mostly from Norway and Spain (Figure 2A), while those with the highest UPF intake were mostly from Lithuania and the UK (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Children with the highest UPF intake were mostly from Lithuania and the UK.
source: Children with the highest KIDMED scores were mostly from Norway and Spain (Figure 2A), while those with the highest UPF intake were mostly from Lithuania and the UK (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: KIDMED and UPF intake exhibited an opposite pattern of association for most of the metabolites (30 out of 43).
source: KIDMED and UPF intake exhibited an opposite pattern of association for most of the metabolites (30 out of 43).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: A panel of four metabolites (hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, urea, and sucrose) related to both diet quality indicators (KIDMED and UPF intake) after controlling for FDR (FDR-corrected p value <0.05).
source: After controlling for FDR (FDR-corrected p value <0.05), we found that a panel of four metabolites related to both diet quality indicators. Specifically, a higher KIDMED score was associated with higher levels of hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea and with lower levels of sucrose; UPF intake exhibited opposite associations with these four metabolites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: A higher KIDMED score was associated with higher levels of hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea and with lower levels of sucrose.
source: Specifically, a higher KIDMED score was associated with higher levels of hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea and with lower levels of sucrose; UPF intake exhibited opposite associations with these four metabolites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: UPF intake exhibited opposite associations with hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, urea, and sucrose compared to KIDMED score.
source: Specifically, a higher KIDMED score was associated with higher levels of hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea and with lower levels of sucrose; UPF intake exhibited opposite associations with these four metabolites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: A higher KIDMED score was also associated with higher acetate and pantothenic acid concentrations.
source: A higher KIDMED score was also associated with higher acetate and pantothenic acid concentrations, while tyrosine and valine concentrations were inversely associated with UPF intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Tyrosine and valine concentrations were inversely associated with UPF intake.
source: A higher KIDMED score was also associated with higher acetate and pantothenic acid concentrations, while tyrosine and valine concentrations were inversely associated with UPF intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The combination of four metabolites associated with both diet quality indicators performed better than individual metabolites in discriminating children with high and low KIDMED scores and UPF intake.
source: ROC curve analyses showed that the combination of four metabolites associated with both diet quality indicators performed better than individual metabolites in discriminating children with high and low KIDMED scores and UPF intake (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The discriminative ability of the four-metabolite panel was equal or even greater to that of established sociodemographic factors previously linked to diet quality in childhood.
source: The discriminative ability of this metabolite panel was not improved with the addition of urinary metabolites specifically linked to each diet quality indicator and was equal or even greater to that of established sociodemographic factors previously linked to diet quality in childhood.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: A higher KIDMED score was associated with lower C-peptide.
source: We found that a higher KIDMED score was associated with lower C-peptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Compared to a low KIDMED score (<1), children with a moderate score (1–4) had a 28% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −27.7, 95% CI: −49.6 to 3.9).
source: Specifically, compared to a low KIDMED score (<1), children with a moderate score (1–4) had a 28% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −27.7, 95% CI: −49.6 to 3.9) and those with a high score (>4) had a 39% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −39.0, 95% CI: −60.6 to −5.7) (p-trend = 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Children with a high KIDMED score (>4) had a 39% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −39.0, 95% CI: −60.6 to −5.7) compared to those with a low score (<1).
source: Specifically, compared to a low KIDMED score (<1), children with a moderate score (1–4) had a 28% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −27.7, 95% CI: −49.6 to 3.9) and those with a high score (>4) had a 39% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −39.0, 95% CI: −60.6 to −5.7) (p-trend = 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: There was a significant trend (p-trend = 0.03) in the association between KIDMED score and C-peptide concentration.
source: Specifically, compared to a low KIDMED score (<1), children with a moderate score (1–4) had a 28% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −27.7, 95% CI: −49.6 to 3.9) and those with a high score (>4) had a 39% lower C-peptide concentration (percent change: −39.0, 95% CI: −60.6 to −5.7) (p-trend = 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: UPF intake was positively associated with C-peptide concentration.
source: An opposite association was observed for UPF intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and inferred from the context.

claim: Compared to children at the lowest quartile of UPF intake (<18% of total daily food intake), children at the second quartile (18% to <23% of total daily food intake) had a 24% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 24.3, 95% CI: −6.4 to 65.2).
source: Compared to children at the lowest quartile of UPF intake (<18% of total daily food intake), children at the second quartile (18% to <23% of total daily food intake) had a 24% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 24.3, 95% CI: −6.4 to 65.2), those at the third quartile (23% to < 29% of total daily food intake) had a 39% higher concentration (percent change: 38.5, 95% CI: 3.8–84.9), and those at the fourth quartile (≥29% of total daily food intake) had a 46% higher concentration (percent change: 46.0, 95% CI: 8.1–97.3) (p-trend = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Children at the third quartile of UPF intake (23% to < 29% of total daily food intake) had a 39% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 38.5, 95% CI: 3.8–84.9) compared to those at the lowest quartile.
source: Compared to children at the lowest quartile of UPF intake (<18% of total daily food intake), children at the second quartile (18% to <23% of total daily food intake) had a 24% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 24.3, 95% CI: −6.4 to 65.2), those at the third quartile (23% to < 29% of total daily food intake) had a 39% higher concentration (percent change: 38.5, 95% CI: 3.8–84.9), and those at the fourth quartile (≥29% of total daily food intake) had a 46% higher concentration (percent change: 46.0, 95% CI: 8.1–97.3) (p-trend = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Children at the fourth quartile of UPF intake (≥29% of total daily food intake) had a 46% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 46.0, 95% CI: 8.1–97.3) compared to those at the lowest quartile.
source: Compared to children at the lowest quartile of UPF intake (<18% of total daily food intake), children at the second quartile (18% to <23% of total daily food intake) had a 24% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 24.3, 95% CI: −6.4 to 65.2), those at the third quartile (23% to < 29% of total daily food intake) had a 39% higher concentration (percent change: 38.5, 95% CI: 3.8–84.9), and those at the fourth quartile (≥29% of total daily food intake) had a 46% higher concentration (percent change: 46.0, 95% CI: 8.1–97.3) (p-trend = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: There was a significant trend (p-trend = 0.01) in the association between UPF intake and C-peptide concentration.
source: Compared to children at the lowest quartile of UPF intake (<18% of total daily food intake), children at the second quartile (18% to <23% of total daily food intake) had a 24% higher C-peptide concentration (percent change: 24.3, 95% CI: −6.4 to 65.2), those at the third quartile (23% to < 29% of total daily food intake) had a 39% higher concentration (percent change: 38.5, 95% CI: 3.8–84.9), and those at the fourth quartile (≥29% of total daily food intake) had a 46% higher concentration (percent change: 46.0, 95% CI: 8.1–97.3) (p-trend = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: There was no evidence of interaction between the diet quality indicators (KIDMED and UPF intake).
source: There was no evidence of interaction between the diet quality indicators (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1h.

claim: There was no significant between-cohort heterogeneity in the associations of diet quality indicators with C-peptide (I2 <18%, p for heterogeneity >0.29).
source: When we examined the associations separately in each cohort, we found no significant between-cohort heterogeneity (I2 <18%, p for heterogeneity >0.29) (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: There was no evidence that the observed associations between diet quality and C-peptide differed by the sex of the children or their weight status.
source: We also found no evidence that the observed associations differed by the sex of the children or their weight status (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1i.

claim: The metabolite scores for KIDMED were associated with lower C-peptide.
source: When we examined the associations with the metabolite scores for each diet quality indicator, we found that the scores for KIDMED were associated with lower C-peptide, while opposite associations were observed with the metabolite scores for UPF (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1j.

claim: The metabolite scores for UPF were associated with higher C-peptide.
source: When we examined the associations with the metabolite scores for each diet quality indicator, we found that the scores for KIDMED were associated with lower C-peptide, while opposite associations were observed with the metabolite scores for UPF (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 1j.

claim: Higher levels of sucrose were associated with higher C-peptide levels.
source: In the pairwise associations between the individual urinary metabolites linked to KIDMED or UPF intake and C-peptide, we found that higher levels of sucrose were associated with higher C-peptide levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: This is the first study of European children that identified a panel of urinary metabolites associated with diet quality, as assessed by a Mediterranean diet adherence score (KIDMED) and UPF intake.
source: This is the first study of European children that identified a panel of urinary metabolites associated with diet quality, as assessed by a Mediterranean diet adherence score (KIDMED) and UPF intake.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: For both diet quality indices, KIDMED score and UPF intake, there was a common panel of four metabolites exhibiting an opposite pattern of association: higher levels of hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea, and lower levels of sucrose were concomitant with a higher KIDMED score and lower UPF intake.
source: For both diet quality indices, KIDMED score and UPF intake, there was a common panel of four metabolites exhibiting an opposite pattern of association: higher levels of hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea, and lower levels of sucrose were concomitant with a higher KIDMED score and lower UPF intake.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Urinary metabolites that reflected diet quality indicators were also associated with C-peptide levels, a well-known marker of β-cell function and insulin resistance.
source: Moreover, these urinary metabolites that reflected these diet quality indicators, were also associated with C-peptide levels, a well-known marker of β-cell function and insulin resistance (Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to Patel et al., 2012.

claim: The Mediterranean diet is characterized by high intake of fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and whole grain products, fish and low intakes of red meat and sweets.
source: The Mediterranean diet is characterized by high intake of fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and whole grain products, fish and low intakes of red meat and sweets, and it has long been appraised for its cardiometabolic benefits, even in children. (Chatzi et al., 2017b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chatzi et al., 2017b.

claim: The Mediterranean diet has long been appraised for its cardiometabolic benefits, even in children.
source: The Mediterranean diet is characterized by high intake of fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and whole grain products, fish and low intakes of red meat and sweets, and it has long been appraised for its cardiometabolic benefits, even in children. (Chatzi et al., 2017b)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chatzi et al., 2017b.

claim: High consumption of UPF has been proposed to lead to metabolic dysregulation.
source: Effects of UPF consumption are likely to be the result of synergistic effects of many food ingredient compound and characteristics, and high consumption of UPF has been proposed to lead to metabolic dysregulation (Srour et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Srour et al., 2020.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous metabolomics studies conducted in adults.
source: Our finding are consistent with previous metabolomics studies conducted in adults (Garcia-Perez et al., 2017; Garcia-Perez et al., 2020; Almanza-Aguilera et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garcia-Perez et al., 2017; Garcia-Perez et al., 2020; Almanza-Aguilera et al., 2017.

claim: The urine metabolic profile for the diet most concordant with WHO healthy eating guidelines showed systematic differences for a total of 28 metabolites, including increased levels of acetate, hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea, compared to the diet that diverted from the healthy guidelines.
source: The urine metabolic profile for the diet most concordant with the guidelines, characterized by high intakes of dietary fiber (through fruits, vegetables, and whole grain cereal products) and low intakes of fat, sugar, and salt showed systematic differences for a total of 28 metabolites, including increased levels of acetate, hippurate, N-methylnicotinic acid, and urea, compared to the diet that diverted from the healthy guidelines (Garcia-Perez et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Garcia-Perez et al., 2017.

claim: The PREDIMED study used NMR to define urinary biomarkers associated with a high adherence to a Mediterranean diet pattern in adults and the proposed biomarkers included higher levels of urea.
source: The PREDIMED study also used NMR to define urinary biomarkers associated with a high adherence to a Mediterranean diet pattern in adults and the proposed biomarkers also included higher levels of urea (Almanza-Aguilera et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Almanza-Aguilera et al., 2017.

claim: This study is the first to show the urinary metabolic footprint of total UPF intake.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to show the urinary metabolic footprint of total UPF intake, and also the first to show that urine NMR-derived scores of diet quality are reflective of a key biomarker of metabolic health, C-peptide, in healthy children.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: This study is the first to show that urine NMR-derived scores of diet quality are reflective of a key biomarker of metabolic health, C-peptide, in healthy children.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to show the urinary metabolic footprint of total UPF intake, and also the first to show that urine NMR-derived scores of diet quality are reflective of a key biomarker of metabolic health, C-peptide, in healthy children.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature at the time of writing and data from the study.

claim: Elevated levels of added sugars could lead to elevated glucose load in the human body, which in turn can lead to an increase in glycemic response and, thus, C-peptide production in healthy populations.
source: Elevated levels of added sugars could lead to elevated glucose load in the human body, which in turn can lead to an increase in glycemic response and, thus, C-peptide production in healthy populations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established scientific knowledge.

claim: There is only one previous study from Mexico examining the relation of diet to C-peptide in children.
source: To the best of our knowledge, there is only one previous study from Mexico examining the relation of diet to C-peptide in children (Perng et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature at the time of writing and a citation to Perng et al., 2017.

claim: A previous study from Mexico showed that adherence to a prudent dietary pattern characterized by food groups commonly consumed in Mediterranean diet (vegetables, fruit, fish, and legumes) was associated with low C-peptide levels in boys.
source: Similar to our findings, this study showed that adherence to a prudent dietary pattern characterized by food groups commonly consumed in Mediterranean diet (vegetables, fruit, fish, and legumes) was associated with low C-peptide levels in boys.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the context and citation to Perng et al., 2017.

claim: Previous studies in children and adults reported that low adherence to a healthy dietary pattern or high consumption of specific UPFs (sugar-sweetened beverages and ultra-processed meat) were associated with impaired glucose regulation and insulin resistance.
source: Regarding other markers of glucose regulation, our findings are in line with previous studies in children and adults reporting that low adherence to a healthy dietary pattern or high consumption of specific UPFs (sugar-sweetened beverages and ultra-processed meat) were associated with impaired glucose regulation and insulin resistance (Manios et al., 2010; Asghari et al., 2016; Chan She Ping-Delfos et al., 2015; McKeown et al., 2018; Ley et al., 2014; Fiorito et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manios et al., 2010; Asghari et al., 2016; Chan She Ping-Delfos et al., 2015; McKeown et al., 2018; Ley et al., 2014; Fiorito et al., 2009.

claim: Hippurate is a normal component of urine, a metabolic product of phenolic compounds which are present in various dietary sources.
source: Regarding the other urinary metabolites reflecting diet quality, hippurate is a normal component of urine, a metabolic product of phenolic compounds which are present in various dietary sources.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hippurate is a biomarker of fruit/vegetable intake, as it has been confirmed in previous studies in healthy children, adolescents and adults.
source: It is also a biomarker of fruit/vegetable intake, as it has been confirmed in previous studies in healthy children, adolescents (Lau et al., 2018; Krupp et al., 2012) and adults (Edmands et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lau et al., 2018; Krupp et al., 2012; Edmands et al., 2011.

claim: N-methylnicotinic acid (trigonelline) is a product of the metabolism of niacin (vitamin B3).
source: N-methylnicotinic acid (trigonelline) is a product of the metabolism of niacin (vitamin B3) and a biomarker of various dietary sources like legumes (Sri Harsha et al., 2018) and fruits (Lau et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: N-methylnicotinic acid is a biomarker of various dietary sources like legumes and fruits.
source: N-methylnicotinic acid (trigonelline) is a product of the metabolism of niacin (vitamin B3) and a biomarker of various dietary sources like legumes (Sri Harsha et al., 2018) and fruits (Lau et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sri Harsha et al., 2018 and Lau et al., 2018.

claim: Urea is the principal end product of amino acids and protein catabolism and a potential marker of protein intake from food.
